content_html:
Lubricating a garage door can reduce noise and wear at hinges, compatible rollers, and springs when the manufacturer allows it, but it does not correct an unbalanced door or damaged cable. Use the lubricant specified for garage-door hardware, apply it sparingly, and stay out of spring and cable adjustments that require disassembly or tension changes.

Clean dirt and dust before lubricating

With the door closed and the opener disconnected as the manual directs, wipe accessible hinges and surfaces. Adding lubricant over dirt-loaded grease creates abrasive paste and makes cracks or wear harder to see.

Lubricate pivot points, not tracks like sliding rails

Apply a small amount to hinge pins, metal roller bearings, and other points identified by the manufacturer. Tracks should stay clean and aligned; coating them in grease can trap dirt and does not repair a damaged roller.

Do not dismantle springs, cables, or loaded brackets

Springs store substantial energy, and some brackets remain loaded even when the door is still. You can apply external lubricant if the manual calls for it, but tension adjustments, cable replacement, or removal of loaded hardware are professional work.

Cycle the door and wipe excess

After reconnecting the opener, run the door once or twice to distribute the product. Wipe drips and listen for any remaining localized noise. A bang, frayed cable, or door dropping on one side is not a lubrication problem.
